subject: rocket launch
title: What If One Missing Symbol Destroyed a Rocket? In 1962 It Did

scenes.text: What if a single missing symbol could destroy a spacecraft? In 1962, one did.
July 22, 1962. NASA launches Mariner 1, built to make the first flyby of Venus.
Minutes into the flight, a piece of guidance hardware fails. The software should take over. But one tiny symbol, an overbar, was left out of its equations.
The rocket veers off course, and nothing on the ground can steer it back.
At 293 seconds, a safety officer sends the destruct command, with just six seconds left before the probe would have separated.
The loss: 18.5 million dollars, over 150 million today. Arthur C. Clarke called it the most expensive hyphen in history. Five weeks later, its twin, Mariner 2, launched and reached Venus.

description:
What if one missing character in a computer program could destroy a spacecraft? On 22 July 1962 it happened to Mariner 1, NASA's first probe aimed at Venus.
A guidance hardware failure handed control to software in which an overbar had been left out of the equations. The Atlas-Agena veered off course and was destroyed by range safety 293 seconds after launch, six seconds before the probe was due to separate. The loss was 18.5 million dollars in 1962 money. The review cited a missing 'hyphen', and Arthur C. Clarke called it the most expensive hyphen in history. Mariner 2 launched on 27 August 1962 and reached Venus.
